r: hǎo hàn bù chī yǎn qián kuī
mean: a sensible person backs down rather than lose out on the spot
lit: a real man of courage does not take a beating right in front of his eyes

use.how: A full sentence, often to justify giving in when facing someone stronger: 算了，好汉不吃眼前亏。 Said about yielding, apologising or paying up rather than losing a face-off.

near.diff: 走为上计 means getting away; 好汉不吃眼前亏 means giving in on the spot, for example by apologising or handing something over.

near.t: 留得青山在，不怕没柴烧
near.diff: 留得青山在 is about saving your strength after a big setback; 好汉不吃眼前亏 is about yielding in an immediate confrontation.

cue: Three big drunk men block your way and demand an apology for a bump that was their fault. You apologise anyway, and later tell your friend why.

ctx.s: 对方人多，你就先认个错吧，{好汉不吃眼前亏}。
ctx.en: There are more of them, so just say sorry for now. No sense getting hurt over it.

ctx.s: 他明明没错，却低头道了歉，事后说：“{好汉不吃眼前亏}嘛。”
ctx.en: He wasn't in the wrong, but he apologised anyway, and afterwards said: "Why take a beating on the spot?"

ctx.s: 小偷亮出了刀，他想到{好汉不吃眼前亏}，就把钱包交了出去。
ctx.en: When the thief pulled out a knife, he decided it wasn't worth getting hurt and handed over his wallet.

ctx.s: “你怎么不跟老板理论？”“他正在气头上，{好汉不吃眼前亏}，以后再说。”
ctx.en: "Why didn't you argue with the boss?" "He's furious right now. No point getting burned; I'll bring it up later."

ctx.s: 对方占尽了优势，经理心想{好汉不吃眼前亏}，先让了一步。
ctx.en: The other side held all the cards, so the manager thought it wiser to back down and give a little ground for now.

ctx.s: 爷爷常说，{好汉不吃眼前亏}，硬碰硬只会让自己受伤。
ctx.en: Grandpa always says a wise man doesn't take a loss he can avoid; meeting force with force only gets you hurt.

bad.s: 我昨天吃了很多亏，真是{好汉不吃眼前亏}。
bad.en: (meant: I lost out a lot yesterday)
bad.why: It is advice to back down so as to avoid a loss, not a description of having suffered one.

bad.s: 他面对困难从不退缩，真是{好汉不吃眼前亏}。
bad.en: (meant: he never backs off from difficulty, a true hero)
bad.why: The saying justifies backing down, so it cannot praise someone for standing firm.

r: sān shí liù jì, zǒu wéi shàng jì
mean: when there is no way to win, getting away is the best plan
lit: of the thirty-six stratagems, walking away is the best one

story.text: In the Southern Qi dynasty the general Wang Jingze rose in revolt. Hearing that the crown prince had packed up and was ready to flee, he mocked them: of Lord Tan's thirty-six stratagems, running away was the best, so father and son had better run at once. Lord Tan was Tan Daoji, a general of the earlier Liu Song dynasty remembered for withdrawing his army from the Northern Wei. The famous book called the Thirty-Six Stratagems was compiled much later.

use.how: A full sentence, often jokingly, when someone decides to slip away from a bad or awkward situation: 情况不妙，三十六计，走为上计。

near.diff: 好汉不吃眼前亏 means yielding to avoid a loss on the spot; 走为上计 means physically leaving or escaping.

cue: The host's uncle has started his third long speech of the evening. You and a friend exchange a look and quietly head for the door.

ctx.s: 看到妈妈拿着成绩单走过来，弟弟心想：{三十六计，走为上计}。
ctx.en: Seeing Mum coming over with his report card, my little brother thought: time to make a run for it.

ctx.s: 酒桌上大家又开始劝酒，我说：“{三十六计，走为上计}，先走一步！”
ctx.en: When everyone started pushing drinks again, I said: "The best plan is a quick exit. I'll be off first!"

ctx.s: “那个推销员又来了！”“快，{三十六计，走为上计}！”
ctx.en: "That salesman's coming back!" "Quick, let's get out of here!"

ctx.s: 敌人太多，硬拼没有胜算，将军下令：{三十六计，走为上计}。
ctx.en: The enemy far outnumbered them and a fight could not be won, so the general ordered a retreat: getting away was the best plan.

ctx.s: 明知这场争论赢不了，他用了{三十六计，走为上计}这一招，找借口离开了会场。
ctx.en: Knowing he couldn't win the argument, he used the oldest trick there is: he made an excuse and left the meeting.

ctx.s: 公司已经半年发不出工资了，{三十六计，走为上计}，他开始找新工作。
ctx.en: The company hadn't paid wages for half a year. Getting out was the best move, so he started looking for a new job.

bad.s: 今天天气很好，{三十六计，走为上计}，我们去公园散步吧。
bad.en: (meant: the weather is nice, let's go for a walk in the park)
bad.why: The "going" here means escaping trouble you cannot win, not going out for a walk.

bad.s: 这次考试我准备了很多方法，{三十六计，走为上计}。
bad.en: (meant: I have prepared lots of strategies for this exam)
bad.why: It does not praise having many plans; it says that the best plan of all is to run away.

r: yī shān bù róng èr hǔ
mean: two strong rivals cannot share one place of power
lit: one mountain cannot hold two tigers

use.how: A full sentence or after 真是, said about two strong people competing for the same top position, where one must go: 两个人都想当老大，一山不容二虎。

cue: After a merger, two star managers are both promised the director's job. Within a month one of them resigns, and nobody is surprised.

ctx.s: 两个队长都想说了算，{一山不容二虎}，球队天天吵架。
ctx.en: Both captains wanted to be in charge. There wasn't room for two of them, and the team argued every day.

ctx.s: 公司合并后，两位总经理只能留一位，{一山不容二虎}嘛。
ctx.en: After the merger only one of the two general managers could stay. There's no room for two at the top.

ctx.s: “他们俩怎么总是对着干？”“都想当老大呗，{一山不容二虎}。”
ctx.en: "Why are those two always at each other's throats?" "They both want to be top dog. One mountain can't hold two tigers."

ctx.s: 两只公猫在一个家里天天打架，真是{一山不容二虎}。
ctx.en: The two tomcats fight every day in the same house. There really isn't room for both of them.

ctx.s: 乐队里有两个都想当主唱的明星，{一山不容二虎}，乐队很快就解散了。
ctx.en: The band had two stars who both wanted to be lead singer. Neither would give way, and the band soon broke up.

ctx.s: 历史上很多联盟最后破裂，原因往往是{一山不容二虎}。
ctx.en: Many alliances in history eventually fell apart, often because two strong leaders could not share power.

bad.s: 我家有两只猫，{一山不容二虎}，它们关系很好。
bad.en: (meant: we have two cats and they get on well)
bad.why: It says two rivals cannot live side by side, so it cannot describe two who get along.

bad.s: 他一个人做两份工作，真是{一山不容二虎}。
bad.en: (meant: he can't manage two jobs at once)
bad.why: It is about two strong rivals for one position, not one person juggling two tasks.

r: yī gè bā zhang pāi bu xiǎng
mean: it takes two to quarrel; both sides share the blame
lit: one palm on its own cannot make a clap

use.how: A full sentence, said after a quarrel or fight to refuse to blame only one side: 吵架这种事，一个巴掌拍不响。

cue: Two children run to their mother, each insisting the other started the fight. Without asking who hit first, she sends both to their rooms.

ctx.s: 你们俩打架，{一个巴掌拍不响}，都有错。
ctx.en: You two were fighting. It takes two, so you're both in the wrong.

ctx.s: 妈妈不听哥哥解释，只说：“{一个巴掌拍不响}，你们俩都去罚站。”
ctx.en: Mum wouldn't listen to my brother's excuses and just said: "It takes two to fight. Both of you, go and stand in the corner."

ctx.s: “都是他不讲理！”“{一个巴掌拍不响}，你就一点问题都没有吗？”
ctx.en: "It's all because he's unreasonable!" "It takes two to quarrel. Are you saying you did nothing wrong at all?"

ctx.s: 夫妻吵架，{一个巴掌拍不响}，别只怪你老公一个人。
ctx.en: When a couple fights, it takes two. Don't just blame your husband.

ctx.s: 邻居们都说是他先动手，可我觉得{一个巴掌拍不响}。
ctx.en: The neighbours all say he threw the first punch, but I think both sides played a part.

ctx.s: 两个部门的矛盾闹了很久，领导认为{一个巴掌拍不响}，让双方都写检讨。
ctx.en: The feud between the two departments had dragged on for ages. The boss decided both were to blame and had each side write a self-criticism.

bad.s: 他在路上被一个陌生人无故打了，真是{一个巴掌拍不响}。
bad.en: (meant: he was hit by a stranger for no reason)
bad.why: It shares the blame between both sides, so it cannot describe an unprovoked attack on an innocent person.

bad.s: 他一句话也不说，教室里安静极了，真是{一个巴掌拍不响}。
bad.en: (meant: he said nothing and the classroom was completely silent)
bad.why: The missing clap is only an image; the saying is about a conflict having two sides, not about silence.

r: qiǎng niǔ de guā bù tián
mean: a relationship or deal that is forced never turns out well
lit: a melon twisted off the vine by force, before it is ripe, is not sweet

use.how: A full sentence, used as advice against forcing a match, a job or a deal on someone unwilling: 他不愿意就算了，强扭的瓜不甜。

near.diff: 天涯何处无芳草 comforts someone after losing a partner; 强扭的瓜不甜 warns against forcing someone who is unwilling.

cue: Parents keep pushing their son to marry a family friend's daughter, though the two have nothing to say to each other. An aunt tells them to stop.

ctx.s: 她不喜欢你，别再追了，{强扭的瓜不甜}。
ctx.en: She doesn't like you, so stop chasing her. You can't force these things.

ctx.s: 孩子对钢琴一点兴趣都没有，你逼他学也没用，{强扭的瓜不甜}。
ctx.en: The child has no interest in the piano at all. Forcing him won't help; nothing good comes of it.

ctx.s: “他要是不愿意来我们公司，就别勉强了。”“对，{强扭的瓜不甜}。”
ctx.en: "If he doesn't want to join our company, let's not push him." "Right, forcing it never works."

ctx.s: 父母硬让他们结婚，结果天天吵架，真是{强扭的瓜不甜}。
ctx.en: Their parents made them marry, and now they quarrel every day. A forced match never turns out well.

ctx.s: 合作要双方自愿，{强扭的瓜不甜}，对方不同意就算了。
ctx.en: A partnership has to be willing on both sides. If they don't agree, let it go; a forced deal is never a good one.

ctx.s: 他把不想留下的员工都放走了，说{强扭的瓜不甜}。
ctx.en: He let every employee who didn't want to stay leave, saying there was no point keeping people against their will.

bad.s: 这家店的水果不新鲜，真是{强扭的瓜不甜}。
bad.en: (meant: this shop's fruit isn't fresh)
bad.why: The melon is only an image; the saying is about forcing an unwilling person, not about the quality of fruit.

bad.s: 他努力了很多年才考上大学，{强扭的瓜不甜}。
bad.en: (meant: he got into university after years of hard work)
bad.why: It warns against forcing someone else's will, not about one's own effort or how hard a goal was to reach.

r: tiān yá hé chù wú fāng cǎo
mean: after a breakup: there are plenty of others out there to love
lit: where, to the ends of the earth, is there no fragrant grass?

story.text: The line comes from a ci poem by the Song poet Su Shi, written to the tune Butterflies Love Flowers, on a spring scene. Late in spring the willow catkins have blown from the branches and grow fewer, and the poet observes that fragrant grass grows everywhere, to the ends of the earth. Later speakers took the fragrant grass to stand for a person to love, and the line became the standard comfort for the heartbroken.

use.how: A full sentence, often followed by 何必单恋一枝花, said to console someone after a breakup or rejection: 别难过了，天涯何处无芳草。

near.diff: 强扭的瓜不甜 warns against forcing someone unwilling; 天涯何处无芳草 comforts someone that there are others to love.

cue: Your best friend was dumped and has stayed in his room for a week. You drag him out to dinner and tell him she is not the only person in the world.

ctx.s: 别哭了，{天涯何处无芳草}，你会遇到更好的人。
ctx.en: Don't cry. There are plenty more fish in the sea; you'll meet someone better.

ctx.s: “她拒绝我了。”“{天涯何处无芳草}，下一个更好！”
ctx.en: "She turned me down." "There are plenty of others out there. The next one will be even better!"

ctx.s: 失恋以后，朋友们都劝他：“{天涯何处无芳草}，何必单恋一枝花？”
ctx.en: After the breakup his friends all told him: "There are plenty of flowers in the world; why pine for just one?"

ctx.s: 表姐离婚后很难过，妈妈安慰她说{天涯何处无芳草}。
ctx.en: My cousin was devastated after her divorce, and Mum comforted her by saying there are plenty of other people out there.

ctx.s: 他嘴上说着{天涯何处无芳草}，心里却还忘不了她。
ctx.en: He kept saying there were plenty of other girls out there, but deep down he still couldn't forget her.

ctx.s: 苏轼的“{天涯何处无芳草}”，本来写的是暮春的景色。
ctx.en: Su Shi's line about fragrant grass everywhere was originally a description of late spring.

bad.s: 他们结婚五十年了，感情很好，真是{天涯何处无芳草}。
bad.en: (meant: they have been happily married for fifty years)
bad.why: It consoles someone who has lost a partner by saying there are others; it cannot praise a lasting marriage.

bad.s: 你妻子刚去世，别太伤心，{天涯何处无芳草}。
bad.en: (meant: to comfort a man whose wife has just died)
bad.why: It is a light comfort for a breakup; said to someone in mourning it sounds heartless and offensive.

t: 千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重
r: qiān lǐ sòng é máo, lǐ qīng qíng yì zhòng
mean: a small gift is precious for the thought behind it
lit: a goose feather sent from a thousand li away: the gift is light, but the feeling behind it is heavy

story.text: A legend tells of Mian Bogao, an envoy sent by the Huihe (Uighur) ruler with a white swan as a gift for Emperor Taizong of Tang. On the long road he stopped at a lake to let the swan bathe, and it flew off, leaving only a feather. Not daring to arrive empty-handed, he presented the feather with a short poem saying the gift was light but the feeling was heavy. The emperor was moved and did not blame him.
story.source: a folk legend set at the Tang court

use.how: A full sentence, said modestly by a giver about a small gift, or warmly by a receiver: 一点小东西，千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重。 Often shortened to 礼轻情意重.

cue: A friend back from her hometown brings you a small jar of her grandmother's homemade chilli sauce and apologises that it's nothing much.

ctx.s: 这是我自己做的小卡片，{千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重}。
ctx.en: This is a little card I made myself. It's not much, but it comes from the heart.

ctx.s: “这么点东西，不好意思。”“哪里，{千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重}！”
ctx.en: "Sorry it's such a small thing." "Not at all, it's the thought that counts!"

ctx.s: 老朋友专门从老家带来一包茶叶，{千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重}，我很感动。
ctx.en: My old friend brought me a packet of tea all the way from his hometown. A small gift, but I was really touched by the thought.

ctx.s: 在国外留学的学生寄来一张明信片，老师笑着说：“{千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重}啊。”
ctx.en: A former student studying abroad sent a postcard, and the teacher smiled: "A small gift from far away, but what a kind thought."

ctx.s: 送礼不一定要贵，{千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重}，心意最重要。
ctx.en: A present doesn't have to be expensive. Even a small gift is precious; it's the thought that matters most.

ctx.s: 孩子们用零花钱给奶奶买了一条围巾，奶奶说这就是{千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重}。
ctx.en: The children bought Grandma a scarf with their pocket money, and she said that was exactly what a small gift with a big heart means.

bad.s: 他送了我一辆新车，真是{千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重}。
bad.en: (meant: he gave me a new car, how generous)
bad.why: It is about a small, cheap gift; an expensive present like a car is the opposite of light.

bad.s: 他只送了我一支笔，真是{千里送鹅毛，礼轻情意重}，太小气了。
bad.en: (meant: he only gave me a pen, how stingy)
bad.why: It values a small gift for its thought, so it cannot be used to complain that someone is mean.

t: 在家靠父母，出门靠朋友
r: zài jiā kào fù mǔ, chū mén kào péng you
mean: away from home, you have to rely on friends for help
lit: at home you rely on your parents; once you leave home you rely on your friends

use.how: A full sentence, said when living or working far from home: to thank people who helped, to ask for help, or to advise making friends: 在家靠父母，出门靠朋友嘛。

near.diff: 远亲不如近邻 says neighbours nearby help more than distant relatives; 在家靠父母，出门靠朋友 is about needing friends once you leave home.

cue: You have just moved to a new city for work and know no one. A classmate's cousin helps you carry your furniture and shows you around. You thank him.

ctx.s: 刚到北京时，多亏同学帮忙，真是{在家靠父母，出门靠朋友}。
ctx.en: When I first got to Beijing, my classmates helped me so much. Away from home, you really do depend on friends.

ctx.s: “以后有事尽管找我。”“太好了，{在家靠父母，出门靠朋友}嘛！”
ctx.en: "If you ever need anything, just ask me." "Great! Away from home, friends are all you've got!"

ctx.s: 爸爸送我上火车时叮嘱：“{在家靠父母，出门靠朋友}，要和同学搞好关系。”
ctx.en: Seeing me off at the train, Dad told me: "Away from home you'll need your friends, so get on well with your classmates."

ctx.s: 他在国外生病时，是几个朋友轮流照顾他，{在家靠父母，出门靠朋友}啊。
ctx.en: When he fell ill abroad, a few friends took turns looking after him. Far from home, friends are your family.

ctx.s: 新来的同事请大家吃饭，说：“{在家靠父母，出门靠朋友}，以后请多关照！”
ctx.en: The new colleague treated everyone to dinner and said: "Away from home I'll be relying on you all, so please look out for me!"

ctx.s: 在外地打工的老乡们常常互相帮忙，因为大家都明白{在家靠父母，出门靠朋友}。
ctx.en: People from the same hometown working far away often help each other out, because they all know that away from home you depend on friends.

bad.s: 我第一次去朋友家玩，{在家靠父母，出门靠朋友}。
bad.en: (meant: I visited a friend's home for the first time)
bad.why: "Going out" here means living away from home, and the saying is about needing help; it does not describe a visit.

bad.s: 他从来不帮朋友，因为{在家靠父母，出门靠朋友}。
bad.en: (meant: he never helps his friends)
bad.why: The saying stresses that friends must help each other away from home, so it cannot excuse refusing to help.

r: yī huí shēng, èr huí shú
mean: awkward the first time, at ease the second: familiarity comes fast
lit: a stranger the first time, familiar the second time

use.how: A full sentence, said to put someone at ease when meeting people or doing something for the first time: 别紧张，一回生，二回熟。

near.diff: 万事开头难 stresses that starting is hard; 一回生，二回熟 reassures that it already feels easy the next time.

cue: A shy new neighbour barely speaks at your first dinner together. As you see him out, you tell him that next time it will feel like visiting old friends.

ctx.s: 第一次见面有点紧张很正常，{一回生，二回熟}嘛。
ctx.en: It's normal to be a bit nervous the first time you meet. Next time you'll feel at home.

ctx.s: “我不会用这台机器。”“没关系，{一回生，二回熟}，多用几次就会了。”
ctx.en: "I don't know how to use this machine." "No problem. It's only strange the first time; use it a few times and you'll have it."

ctx.s: 他第一次包饺子包得很难看，奶奶笑着说{一回生，二回熟}。
ctx.en: His first dumplings looked terrible, and Grandma laughed and said he'd get the hang of it next time.

ctx.s: 新来的同事有点拘谨，老张拍拍他的肩说：“{一回生，二回熟}，以后就是自己人了。”
ctx.en: The new colleague was a bit stiff, so Lao Zhang patted him on the shoulder: "First time's always awkward. From now on you're one of us."

ctx.s: 我们第一次合作还不太默契，不过{一回生，二回熟}，下次一定更顺利。
ctx.en: Our first project together wasn't very smooth, but now that we know each other, next time will go much better.

ctx.s: 第一次去那家医院找了半天，{一回生，二回熟}，现在我很快就能找到科室。
ctx.en: The first time I went to that hospital I spent ages looking around, but once you've been there it's easy; now I find the right department in no time.

bad.s: 我们是二十年的老朋友了，真是{一回生，二回熟}。
bad.en: (meant: we have been close friends for twenty years)
bad.why: It is about the first awkward meetings becoming easy, not about a friendship that is already long and deep.

bad.s: 这道菜我做了很多次，还是很生，{一回生，二回熟}。
bad.en: (meant: I've cooked this dish many times and it's still underdone)
bad.why: The words for raw and cooked here mean unfamiliar and familiar; the saying is not about food being undercooked.

mean: a clash or fight can be the start of a friendship
lit: without a fight, they would never have come to know each other

story.text: In the novel Water Margin, the hot-tempered Li Kui picks a fight with the fishmonger Zhang Shun on the bank of the Xunyang River. Li Kui beats him on land, but Zhang Shun lures him into the water and nearly drowns him. Song Jiang and Dai Zong step in and introduce the two, and Dai Zong quotes a common saying, in the slightly longer form "bu da bu cheng xiangshi": without a fight, no friendship. From then on the two are firm friends.

use.how: A full sentence or after 真是 or 这叫, said by or about people who became friends after a quarrel or fight: 我们俩是不打不相识。

cue: Two drivers have a minor crash and shout at each other, then discover they come from the same small town. Now they go fishing together every weekend.

ctx.s: 我和他小时候打过一架，后来成了好朋友，真是{不打不相识}。
ctx.en: He and I had a fight as kids and then became best friends. Sometimes a fight is how friendships start.

ctx.s: “你们俩是怎么认识的？”“说来好笑，是吵架吵出来的，{不打不相识}嘛。”
ctx.en: "How did you two meet?" "Funny story, it started with a row. We only became friends because we fought!"

ctx.s: 他和邻居因为停车位吵过一次，没想到{不打不相识}，现在常常一起喝茶。
ctx.en: He once had a row with his neighbour over a parking space; who'd have thought it would make them friends? Now they often have tea together.

ctx.s: 两个球员在场上发生冲突，赛后却握手拥抱，真是{不打不相识}。
ctx.en: The two players clashed on the pitch, but after the game they shook hands and hugged. A fight can be the start of a friendship.

ctx.s: 网上争论过的两个人后来见了面，笑着说彼此是{不打不相识}。
ctx.en: Two people who had argued online later met in person and laughed that their quarrel was how they became friends.

ctx.s: 两家公司打了三年官司，最后却成了合作伙伴，这叫{不打不相识}。
ctx.en: The two companies fought each other in court for three years and ended up as partners. That's how a clash turns into a friendship.

bad.s: 我们俩天天打架，一直合不来，真是{不打不相识}。
bad.en: (meant: we fight every day and have never got on)
bad.why: The clash must lead to friendship; it cannot describe two people who stay enemies.

bad.s: 我和他第一次见面就很投缘，{不打不相识}。
bad.en: (meant: we hit it off the moment we met)
bad.why: There must be a conflict first; without a clash the saying does not apply.
